summary:
Aruba is a constituent territory within the Kingdom of the Netherlands and stands under that framework; the island's own Criminal Code (Wetboek van Strafrecht / Kódigo Penal), enacted in 2012, carries the anti-discrimination provisions in force here. Article 1:221 defines discrimination as any form of discrimination, exclusion, restriction or preference that has the purpose or effect of affecting the recognition, enjoyment or exercise of human rights and fundamental liberties in political, economic, social or cultural fields or in other areas of social life, and Articles 2:61 and 2:62 set penalties ranging from fines to one year of imprisonment. The enumerated grounds cover heterosexual or homosexual orientation only. Gender identity and gender expression are not addressed, and no transgender-specific provision is cited in the sources.

Same-sex sexual activity is legal for both male and female forms, and the age of consent is 16, equal for heterosexual and homosexual intercourse. This is the only youth-specific legal threshold in the record; no findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources.

Partner recognition is established at two levels. On 8 September 2016 the Aruban Parliament voted 11 to 5, with four abstentions per the Associated Press account of 9 September 2016, to extend civil-code marriage articles to registered partnerships open to both opposite-sex and same-sex couples, granting spousal pension and emergency medical decision rights. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 12 July 2024, when the Supreme Court of the Netherlands upheld the Appeals Court decision barring discrimination based on sexual orientation in the ruling that made same-sex marriage legal in Aruba. Since the Dutch Supreme Court ruling of 13 April 2007, Aruba must recognize same-sex marriages registered in the Netherlands and in Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 was rejected after tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024, immediately before the July 2024 ruling. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship is dealing with a regime whose protections are written in terms of sexual orientation alone.

On 22 April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments endorsed prompt equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Aruba's own representation at that meeting acknowledged that strict conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth on the island, who were stigmatized as disordered.

Harassment has been documented. Charlene and Esther Oduber-Lamer reported frequent harassment and having rocks thrown at them during their court challenge (2004–2007) that forced Aruba and the other Dutch Caribbean islands to recognize same-sex marriage. The Aruban government was particularly vocal in opposing same-sex marriage during that court challenge, and the Roman Catholic Church, the island's largest denomination, contributed to mainstream societal opposition to LGBT rights. The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record is from that 2004–2007 period; no later instance is documented.

Several specific gay bars and clubs operate in the capital city of Oranjestad, and various venues, hotels and restaurants cater to or advertise as 'LGBT-friendly'. Numerous LGBT associations operate, including Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba. The last is quoted: 'Aruba has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official.'
tangentialFactors:
The official Aruba tourism board markets the island as an established LGBT destination, positioning feeling 'safe, secure, and welcome' as the foundation of the offering and quoting a repeat visitor of nearly 20 years who reports never encountering mistreatment or discrimination based on sexual orientation. This is the destination's own marketer speaking, not independent evidence, but it documents mainstream tourism positioning.

A cultural report edited in January 2017 describes Aruba as tolerant and mostly open, with a smaller and quieter out-and-proud LGBT population than Curaçao, and identifies Catholic influence as the main brake on further change. The same report notes that the government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands.

Religious and cultural opposition was strong enough in 2016 that the registered-partnership bill passed only after a 2.5-year campaign, and a same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2022 failed on tied parliamentary votes in May and June 2024.
localsOnly:
Same-sex adoption is legal in Aruba, per the cultural report edited in January 2017.

The registered-partnership campaign ran 2.5 years, with openly-gay MP Desirée de Sousa-Croes as sponsor, introducing the bill in August 2016, and an Igualdad Aruba petition at nearly 20,000 signatures.

Resident-facing organisations include Equality Aruba (Igualdad Aruba), Equal Rights Aruba and Alternative Lifestyle Federation Aruba, alongside several gay bars and clubs in Oranjestad.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether gender identity or gender expression is recognised anywhere in Aruban law is unresolved in these sources: the Criminal Code grounds enumerated in Article 1:221 cover sexual orientation only, and no transgender-specific provision is cited. Whether any separate instrument addresses gender markers, identity documents or legal gender recognition is not sourced here.

No findings on education, schools, or minors' access to services or documentation appear in the sources; the age of consent of 16 is the only youth-specific threshold given.

No trans-specific violence or killing statistics for Aruba appear in this inventory, and no per-capita or population denominator is available for any figure, so no comparative risk ranking can be drawn.

The most recent documented incident of anti-LGBT harassment in this record dates from the 2004–2007 court challenge; no later instance is documented, and the absence of a later documented case is not evidence that none occurs.

The tourism board's safety claims are self-description by the destination's marketer and are not independent verification.
